grammarPairs.rule: For numbers 3–10, a masculine counted noun takes the feminine-looking number form with tāʾ marbūṭa.

grammarPairs.rule: In date phrases after فِي (fī), the ordinal is genitive.

grammarPairs.rule: Use الأُولَى (al-ūlā) for feminine “the first.”
grammarPairs.example: Complete “the first unit”: الوَحْدَةُ ___ (al-waḥdatu ___).

grammarPairs.rule: Percentages often use فِي المِئَةِ (fī al-miʾati) after the number.

grammarPairs.rule: Clock hours usually use feminine ordinal forms because سَاعَةٌ (sāʿatun) is feminine.

grammarPairs.rule: إِلَّا رُبْعًا (illā rubʿan) means “except a quarter,” used for “a quarter to.”

grammarPairs.rule: The five nouns show nominative with wāw when conditions are met.
grammarPairs.example: Complete “your father came”: جَاءَ ___ (jāʾa ___).

grammarPairs.rule: ذُو (dhū) changes to ذَا (dhā) in the accusative and ذِي (dhī) in the genitive.
grammarPairs.example: Complete “with a man of knowledge”: مَعَ رَجُلٍ ___ عِلْمٍ (maʿa rajulin ___ ʿilmin).

grammarPairs.rule: The genitive form of أَبُوكَ (abūka) is أَبِيكَ (abīka).
grammarPairs.example: Complete “by your father”: بِ___ (bi-___).

grammarPairs.rule: A diptote usually takes fatḥa for genitive when indefinite and not in iḍāfa.

grammarPairs.rule: Many broken plurals on مَفَاعِلُ (mafāʿilu) are diptotes.

grammarPairs.rule: Definiteness with اَلْـ (al-) can restore genitive kasra to a diptote.
grammarPairs.example: Complete “in the mosques”: فِي المَسَاجِد___ (fī al-masājid___).

grammarPairs.rule: In verb-first VSO order, the verb is usually singular even with a plural subject.

grammarPairs.rule: In subject-first order, the verb commonly agrees fully with the topic-subject.

grammarPairs.rule: Nominal sentences can have no present-tense “to be.”

grammarPairs.rule: Human plurals usually keep plural agreement.
grammarPairs.example: Complete “the new female teachers”: المُعَلِّمَاتُ ___ (al-muʿallimātu ___).

grammarPairs.rule: Use meaning, not just plural shape, to decide agreement.
grammarPairs.example: Complete “old mosques”: مَسَاجِدُ ___ (masājidu ___).

grammarPairs.rule: Ḥāl describes the state of a participant during the action.
grammarPairs.example: Complete “the student came smiling”: جَاءَ الطَّالِبُ ___ (jāʾa aṭ-ṭālibu ___).

grammarPairs.rule: Tamyīz specifies an unclear number or measure.
grammarPairs.example: Complete “I have twenty books”: عِنْدِي عِشْرُونَ ___ (ʿindī ʿishrūna ___).

grammarPairs.rule: Use the question test: “how?” points to ḥāl; “what exactly?” points to tamyīz.
grammarPairs.example: Classify جَالِسًا in قَرَأْتُ الكِتَابَ جَالِسًا (qaraʾtu al-kitāba jālisan).

grammarPairs.rule: After كَانَ (kāna), the predicate is accusative.

grammarPairs.rule: After إِنَّ (inna), the noun is accusative and the predicate remains nominative.
grammarPairs.example: Complete “indeed, the weather is cold”: إِنَّ الجَو___ بَارِدٌ (inna al-jaww___ bāridun).

grammarPairs.rule: Do not mix the two systems: kāna accusative predicate; inna accusative noun.
grammarPairs.example: Choose the ending in إِنَّ الطَّالِب___ مُجْتَهِدٌ (inna aṭ-ṭālib___ mujtahidun).

grammarPairs.rule: Many Form I place/time nouns use مَفْعَلٌ (mafʿalun) or مَفْعِلٌ (mafʿilun).
grammarPairs.example: Complete “entrance” from دَخَلَ (dakhala): ___ (___).

grammarPairs.rule: Context distinguishes mīmī verbal noun from place/time noun.
grammarPairs.example: Classify مَدْخَلُ in مَدْخَلُ البِنَايَةِ وَاسِعٌ (madkhalu al-bināyati wāsiʿun).

grammarPairs.rule: مَوْعِدٌ (mawʿidun) can name an appointed time or appointment.
grammarPairs.example: Complete “we have an appointment”: لَنَا ___ (lanā ___).

grammarPairs.rule: رَحْ (raḥ) is a common Levantine-style future marker before the imperfect verb.
grammarPairs.example: Complete “I will go”: رَحْ ___ (raḥ ___).

grammarPairs.rule: عَمْ (ʿam) marks ongoing action in many Levantine varieties.

grammarPairs.rule: Dialect particles vary, but their position before the verb is a strong clue.
grammarPairs.example: Classify حَسَافِرْ (ḥa-sāfir).

grammarPairs.rule: At the beginning of a word, hamza with kasra is written below alif as إِ.
grammarPairs.example: Choose the correct beginning for ___سْمٌ (ʾismun) — name.

grammarPairs.rule: A middle hamza often takes the seat of the strongest neighboring vowel: kasra, then ḍamma, then fatḥa.
grammarPairs.example: Complete the passive verb: سُ___لَ (suʾila) — he was asked.

grammarPairs.rule: Tāʾ marbūṭa is pronounced -at when connected, but often -ah or -a when pausing.
grammarPairs.example: Read in connection: طَالِبَةٌ جَدِيدَةٌ = ___.

grammarPairs.rule: When a suffix attaches to a word ending in ة, the written form changes to ت before the suffix.
grammarPairs.example: Add her to مَدْرَسَةٌ (madrasatun) — school: ___ .

grammarPairs.rule: Sun letters assimilate the l of the definite article and take shadda.
grammarPairs.example: Read the definite noun: الدَّرْسُ = ___ .

grammarPairs.rule: Moon letters keep the l of الْـ (al-) — the in pronunciation.
grammarPairs.example: Read the definite noun: الْقَلَمُ = ___ .

grammarPairs.rule: Alif maqṣūra ى is read as final ā, not as y, in words like عَلَى and مُوسَى.
grammarPairs.example: Read عَلَى as ___ .

grammarPairs.rule: Dagger alif marks a long ā that is written above the consonant instead of as a full alif.
grammarPairs.example: The word هٰذَا (hādhā) — this contains ___ .

grammarPairs.rule: A noun with the definite article does not keep tanwīn.
grammarPairs.example: Make بَيْتٌ (baytun) — a house definite: ___ .

grammarPairs.rule: In an iḍāfa, the second noun is genitive.
grammarPairs.example: Complete: كِتَابُ ___ (kitābu ___) — the student's book.

grammarPairs.rule: Loanwords can receive Arabic case endings in fully vocalized MSA.
grammarPairs.example: Add nominative tanwīn to بَنْك (bank) — bank: ___ .

grammarPairs.rule: The nisba ending ـِيٌّ (-iyyun) can turn place names and some borrowed bases into adjectives.
grammarPairs.example: Make كَنَدَا (kanadā) — Canada into Canadian: ___ .

grammarPairs.rule: أَخِيرًا means finally; use حَالِيًّا for currently and فِعْلِيًّا for actually.
grammarPairs.example: Translate currently: ___ .

grammarPairs.rule: Use collocations to disambiguate false friends.
grammarPairs.example: كُلِّيَّةُ الطِّبِّ (kulliyyatu ṭ-ṭibbi) means ___ .

grammarPairs.rule: Polite requests often use مِنْ فَضْلِكَ or لَوْ سَمَحْتَ before the request.
grammarPairs.example: Make this polite: اِفْتَحِ الْبَابَ (iftaḥi l-bāba) — open the door: ___ .

grammarPairs.rule: Titles such as السَّيِّدُ and الدُّكْتُورُ usually precede the name in formal address.
grammarPairs.example: Address Mr. Ahmad formally: ___ .

grammarPairs.rule: Arabizi numbers represent Arabic consonants that Latin letters handle poorly.

grammarPairs.rule: Arabizi is informal and variable; formal MSA should use Arabic script.
grammarPairs.example: For a formal text, write 3arabī as ___ .

grammarPairs.rule: MSA is best for formal writing, while dialect phrases are normal in everyday speech.
grammarPairs.example: Choose the formal written phrase for I do not know: ___ .

grammarPairs.rule: Dialect comparison works best phrase by phrase, because vocabulary, sounds, and grammar can all change.
grammarPairs.example: Egyptian رَايِحْ فِين؟ (rāyiḥ fēn?) corresponds to MSA ___ .

grammarPairs.rule: نُونُ النِّسْوَةِ (nūn an-niswa) marks feminine plural verb agreement, as in يَكْتُبْنَ (yaktubna) and كَتَبْنَ (katabna).
grammarPairs.example: Complete they feminine read the lesson: هُنَّ ___ الدَّرْسَ (hunna ___ ad-darsa).

grammarPairs.rule: With a fronted human feminine plural subject, the verb normally shows feminine plural agreement.
grammarPairs.example: Complete the female students wrote: الطَّالِبَاتُ ___ الرِّسَالَةَ (aṭ-ṭālibātu ___ ar-risālata).

grammarPairs.rule: Dual verbs agree fully with dual pronouns and with dual subjects placed before the verb.
grammarPairs.example: Complete the two engineers are working: الْمُهَنْدِسَانِ ___ (al-muhandisāni ___).

grammarPairs.rule: In dual present forms, the indicative nūn of ـَانِ drops after subjunctive and jussive particles such as لَنْ and لَمْ.
grammarPairs.example: Complete they two did not enter: لَمْ ___ الْبَيْتَ (lam ___ al-bayta).

grammarPairs.rule: Many Arabic collective nouns form a unit noun by adding tāʾ marbūṭa, such as تَمْرٌ (tamrun) to تَمْرَةٌ (tamratun).
grammarPairs.example: Complete one fish: سَمَك___ (samak___).

grammarPairs.rule: اِسْمُ الْجِنْسِ (ism al-jins) names a kind or collective, while اِسْمُ الْوَحْدَةِ (ism al-waḥda) names one unit from it.
grammarPairs.example: Choose the class word in this pair: بَقَرٌ / بَقَرَةٌ (baqarun / baqaratun).

grammarPairs.rule: لَا النَّافِيَةُ لِلْجِنْسِ negates an entire class, and its single indefinite noun is built on fatḥa without tanwīn.
grammarPairs.example: Complete no doubt remains: لَا ___ بَاقٍ (lā ___ bāqin).

grammarPairs.rule: Prohibitive لَا is followed by a jussive verb, while absolute-negation لَا is followed by an indefinite noun.

grammarPairs.rule: الْمَفْعُولُ لِأَجْلِهِ is an accusative verbal noun that gives the reason or purpose of an action.
grammarPairs.example: Complete I studied seeking success: دَرَسْتُ ___ لِلنَّجَاحِ (darastu ___ lin-najāḥi).

grammarPairs.rule: A purpose accusative can often be paraphrased with لِـ plus a verbal noun.
grammarPairs.example: Paraphrase جِئْتُ طَلَبًا لِلْعِلْمِ with لِـ.

grammarPairs.rule: الْبَدَلُ follows the case of الْمُبْدَلُ مِنْهُ, the noun it clarifies or replaces.
grammarPairs.example: Complete I saw your brother Zayd: رَأَيْتُ أَخَاكَ ___ (raʾaytu akhāka ___).

grammarPairs.rule: Part-for-whole badal often contains a pronoun that points back to the whole.
grammarPairs.example: Identify the badal in قَرَأْتُ الْكِتَابَ نِصْفَهُ (qaraʾtu al-kitāba niṣfahu).

grammarPairs.rule: The specification after numbers 11–99 is normally singular accusative.
grammarPairs.example: Complete thirty students: ثَلَاثُونَ ___ (thalāthūna ___).

grammarPairs.rule: After 3–10, the counted noun is usually plural genitive; after 11–99, it is usually singular accusative.
grammarPairs.example: Complete seven books: سَبْعَةُ ___ (sabʿatu ___).

grammarPairs.rule: A simple proper-name vocative is usually built on ḍamma, as in يَا زَيْدُ (yā zaydu).
grammarPairs.example: Complete O Maryam: يَا ___ (yā ___).

grammarPairs.rule: When the vocative is an iḍāfa, the called noun is accusative, as in يَا طَالِبَ الْعِلْمِ.
grammarPairs.example: Complete O owner of the house: يَا ___ الْبَيْتِ (yā ___ al-bayti).

grammarPairs.rule: A tashbīh is an explicit comparison, often with كَـ (ka-), مِثْلُ (mithlu), or كَأَنَّ (ka-anna).
grammarPairs.example: Identify the device: العِلْمُ كَالنُّورِ (al-ʿilmu ka-n-nūri).

grammarPairs.rule: An istiʿāra removes the comparison particle and uses a borrowed image as if it were literal.
grammarPairs.example: Explain أَسَدًا in رَأَيْتُ أَسَدًا يَخْطُبُ (raʾaytu asadan yakhṭubu).

grammarPairs.rule: A kināya gives an indirect clue to the intended meaning while leaving the literal wording possible.
grammarPairs.example: What does هِيَ نَظِيفَةُ اليَدِ (hiya naẓīfatu al-yadi) imply?

grammarPairs.rule: Confirming words such as نَفْسٌ (nafsun) follow the emphasized noun and carry a matching pronoun.
grammarPairs.example: Complete the emphasis: جَاءَتِ المُعَلِّمَةُ ___ (jāʾati al-muʿallimatu ___).

grammarPairs.rule: إِنَّ (inna) emphasizes a nominal sentence and puts its noun in the accusative.
grammarPairs.example: Complete: إِنَّ الطَّالِبَ ___ (inna aṭ-ṭāliba ___).

grammarPairs.rule: إِنَّ plus لَـ can combine for strong confirmation: إِنَّ زَيْدًا لَصَادِقٌ (inna zaydan la-ṣādiqun).
grammarPairs.example: Translate the emphasis: إِنَّ زَيْدًا لَصَادِقٌ (inna zaydan la-ṣādiqun).

grammarPairs.rule: مَا … إِلَّا (mā … illā) restricts the sentence by negating everything except one item.
grammarPairs.example: Translate: مَا نَجَحَ إِلَّا خَالِدٌ (mā najaḥa illā khālidun).

grammarPairs.rule: إِنَّمَا (innamā) marks restriction, but context tells whether the subject, predicate, or another phrase is being limited.

grammarPairs.rule: Restriction often answers an implied contrast: not everyone, not everything, not always, but this one item.

grammarPairs.rule: The answer clause, jawāb ash-sharṭ, states the result of the condition.
grammarPairs.example: Find the answer in مَنْ يَصْبِرْ يَفُزْ (man yaṣbir yafuz).

grammarPairs.rule: Use فَـ before a conditional answer when the answer begins with a nominal sentence, command, question, future marker, qad, lan, or mā.
grammarPairs.example: Complete: إِنْ تَحْتَجْ ___ اسْأَلْنِي (in taḥtaj ___ isʾalnī).

grammarPairs.rule: A plain jussive verbal answer often does not need فَـ: إِنْ تَدْرُسْ تَنْجَحْ (in tadrus tanjaḥ).
grammarPairs.example: Should إِنْ تَدْرُسْ تَنْجَحْ need فَـ before تَنْجَحْ?

grammarPairs.rule: Taqdīm brings a phrase forward for emphasis, but its grammatical role stays the same.
grammarPairs.example: What is إِيَّاكَ in إِيَّاكَ نَعْبُدُ (iyyāka naʿbudu)?

grammarPairs.rule: Fronting often creates a topic-comment feel: as for this phrase, here is what is true about it.

grammarPairs.rule: A fronted object can imply restriction or contrast when context supports it.
grammarPairs.example: What nuance can الكِتَابَ قَرَأْتُ (al-kitāba qaraʾtu) have?

grammarPairs.rule: In a basic verbal sentence, the subject is nominative and the direct object is accusative.
grammarPairs.example: Identify the object in قَرَأَ الطَّالِبُ الكِتَابَ (qaraʾa aṭ-ṭālibu al-kitāba).

grammarPairs.rule: A preposition makes the following noun genitive: فِي المَكْتَبَةِ (fī al-maktabati).
grammarPairs.example: Explain the ending in فِي المَكْتَبَةِ (fī al-maktabati).

grammarPairs.rule: In an iḍāfa, the second noun is genitive even when the first noun has another role in the sentence.
grammarPairs.example: Analyze كِتَابَ الطَّالِبِ in قَرَأْتُ كِتَابَ الطَّالِبِ (qaraʾtu kitāba aṭ-ṭālibi).

grammarPairs.rule: كَادَ (kāda) marks an action that nearly happened and is usually followed by a present verb.
grammarPairs.example: Complete: كَادَ الوَلَدُ ___ (kāda al-waladu ___).

grammarPairs.rule: Verbs of beginning such as شَرَعَ and أَخَذَ are followed by a present verb naming the action begun.
grammarPairs.example: Translate: أَخَذَ الطِّفْلُ يَضْحَكُ (akhadha aṭ-ṭiflu yaḍḥaku).

grammarPairs.rule: عَسَى (ʿasā) expresses hope or expectation and often takes أَنْ plus a subjunctive verb.
grammarPairs.example: Translate: عَسَى اللَّهُ أَنْ يَرْحَمَنَا (ʿasā allāhu an yarḥamanā).

grammarPairs.rule: Across dialects, noun suffixes are possessive and verb suffixes are object pronouns.
grammarPairs.example: Compare كِتَابِي (kitābī) and شَافْنِي (shāfnī).

grammarPairs.rule: Dialect suffixes often keep the same function as MSA suffixes but reduce final vowels.
grammarPairs.example: What changed from كِتَابُكَ (kitābuka) to بَيْتَك (bētak)?

grammarPairs.rule: Many dialects use شَافَ (shāfa) for saw, so object suffixes attach to that stem: شَافْنِي (shāfnī), شُفْتُهْ (shuftu).
grammarPairs.example: Translate: شَافْنِي (shāfnī).

grammarPairs.rule: نُونُ التَّوْكِيدِ الثَّقِيلَةُ (-nna) strongly emphasizes a present verb or command.
grammarPairs.example: Complete: I will surely travel: لَ___ (la-___).

grammarPairs.rule: The prefix لَـ often accompanies energetic verbs in oaths and solemn promises.
grammarPairs.example: Complete: We will certainly help: لَ___ (la-___).

grammarPairs.rule: In prohibitions, نُونُ التَّوْكِيدِ makes the negative command more urgent.
grammarPairs.example: Complete: Do not ever betray: لَا ___ (lā ___).

grammarPairs.rule: ظَنَّ (ẓanna) and similar verbs can take two accusative objects from an original nominal sentence.
grammarPairs.example: Change to I thought: الطَّالِبُ مُجْتَهِدٌ (aṭ-ṭālibu mujtahidun).

grammarPairs.rule: عَلِمَ (ʿalima) may introduce two objects when it means to know that something is so.
grammarPairs.example: Complete: I knew the news was true: عَلِمْتُ ___ ___ (ʿalimtu ___ ___).

grammarPairs.rule: If two accusatives after a mental verb can form a nominal sentence, they are probably its two objects.
grammarPairs.example: Analyze: وَجَدْتُ الْمَسْأَلَةَ سَهْلَةً (wajadtu al-masʾalata sahlatan).

grammarPairs.rule: يَجِبُ أَنْ (yajibu an) is followed by a subjunctive present verb.
grammarPairs.example: Complete: We must arrive: يَجِبُ أَنْ ___ (yajibu an ___).

grammarPairs.rule: Arabic weather verbs often use a real natural subject instead of a dummy it.
grammarPairs.example: Translate naturally: تَسَاقَطَ الثَّلْجُ (tasāqaṭa ath-thalju).

grammarPairs.rule: Do not translate English dummy it mechanically as هُوَ in weather and necessity sentences.
grammarPairs.example: Which is idiomatic for it got hot: اِشْتَدَّ ___ (ishtadda ___).

grammarPairs.rule: أَفْعَلُ مِنْ (afʿalu min) is the regular comparative pattern for more X than.
grammarPairs.example: Complete: The house is bigger than the room: الْبَيْتُ ___ مِنَ الْغُرْفَةِ (al-baytu ___ mina al-ghurfati).

grammarPairs.rule: For colour comparisons, use أَشَدُّ or أَكْثَرُ plus a colour noun such as حُمْرَةً.
grammarPairs.example: Complete: This rose is redder: هٰذِهِ الْوَرْدَةُ ___ حُمْرَةً (hādhihi al-wardatu ___ ḥumratan).

grammarPairs.rule: A superlative often appears as الْأَفْعَلُ or as an iḍāfa such as أَكْبَرُ مَدِينَةٍ.
grammarPairs.example: Complete: the shortest road: الطَّرِيقُ ___ (aṭ-ṭarīqu ___).

grammarPairs.rule: A noun can be indefinite in form but specific in context.
grammarPairs.example: In جَاءَ رَجُلٌ (jāʾa rajulun), is رَجُلٌ necessarily non-specific?

grammarPairs.rule: A definite singular or abstract noun can express a generic category.
grammarPairs.example: Translate generically: الصِّدْقُ فَضِيلَةٌ (aṣ-ṣidqu faḍīlatun).

grammarPairs.rule: Attributive adjectives usually match the noun in definiteness.
grammarPairs.example: Complete: the useful book: الْكِتَابُ ___ (al-kitābu ___).

grammarPairs.rule: ظَرْفُ الزَّمَانِ tells when an action happens and is often accusative.
grammarPairs.example: Find the time adverbial: سَافَرْنَا لَيْلًا (sāfarnā laylan).

grammarPairs.rule: Many place adverbials form iḍāfa, so the noun after them is genitive.
grammarPairs.example: Complete: under the chair: تَحْتَ ___ (taḥta ___).

grammarPairs.rule: A ẓarf is identified by its adverbial function: when or where the action happens.
grammarPairs.example: In نَلْتَقِي بَعْدَ الظُّهْرِ (naltaqī baʿda aẓ-ẓuhri), what is بَعْدَ?

grammarPairs.rule: The exclamation pattern مَا أَفْعَلَهُ often puts the admired noun in the accusative.
grammarPairs.example: Complete: How difficult the question is: مَا أَصْعَبَ ___ (mā aṣʿaba ___).

grammarPairs.rule: نِعْمَ praises and بِئْسَ blames in fixed rhetorical patterns.
grammarPairs.example: Complete: Truthfulness is an excellent trait: نِعْمَ الْخُلُقُ ___ (niʿma al-khuluqu ___).

grammarPairs.rule: أَفْعِلْ بِهِ is another exclamation pattern, as in أَكْرِمْ بِالضَّيْفِ.
grammarPairs.example: Translate: أَحْسِنْ بِالصَّبْرِ (aḥsin biṣ-ṣabri).

grammarPairs.rule: Egyptian إِيهْ (ēh) and Levantine شُو (shū) often correspond to MSA مَاذَا (mādhā).
grammarPairs.example: Match the dialect form for what in Egyptian: إِنْتَ عَايِزْ ___؟ (inta ʿāyiz ___).

grammarPairs.rule: وَيْنْ (wēn) commonly corresponds to MSA أَيْنَ (ayna), while لَيْشْ (lēsh) corresponds to لِمَاذَا (limādhā).
grammarPairs.example: Choose the dialect word for why: ___ تَأَخَّرْتَ؟ (___ taʾakhkharta).

grammarPairs.rule: Keep MSA question words for formal Arabic, and dialect question words for regional speech.
grammarPairs.example: Choose the MSA form for where: ___ الْمَكْتَبُ؟ (___ al-maktabu).

grammarPairs.rule: Locative words such as فَوْقَ (fawqa) — above and تَحْتَ (taḥta) — under normally take a genitive complement.
grammarPairs.example: Complete: الْكِتَابُ فَوْقَ الطَّاوِلَة___ (al-kitābu fawqa aṭ-ṭāwilat___) — the book is above the table.

grammarPairs.rule: When a preposition comes before a locative noun, the locative noun can become genitive too.
grammarPairs.example: Complete: مِنْ تَحْت___ الْكُرْسِيِّ (min taḥt___ al-kursiyyi) — from under the chair.

grammarPairs.rule: Attached pronouns can serve as complements of locative words.
grammarPairs.example: Complete: the key is under it/her — اَلْمِفْتَاحُ ___ (al-miftāḥu ___).

grammarPairs.rule: أَنْ (an) makes the following imperfect verb subjunctive.
grammarPairs.example: Complete: يُمْكِنُكَ أَنْ تَدْخُل___ (yumkinuka an tadkhul___) — you may enter.

grammarPairs.rule: يَجِبُ عَلَى (yajibu ʿalā) marks the person who is obligated.
grammarPairs.example: Complete: يَجِبُ عَلَى الطَّالِب___ أَنْ يَدْرُسَ (yajibu ʿalā aṭ-ṭālib___ an yadrusa).

grammarPairs.rule: لَا بُدَّ مِنْ (lā budda min) is followed by a genitive verbal noun or noun phrase.
grammarPairs.example: Complete: لَا بُدَّ مِنْ مُرَاجَعَة___ الدَّرْسِ (lā budda min murājaʿat___ ad-darsi).

grammarPairs.rule: Quoted nominal speech after قَالَ (qāla) often begins with إِنَّ (inna).
grammarPairs.example: Complete: قَالَ الْمُعَلِّمُ: ___ الدَّرْسَ سَهْلٌ (qāla al-muʿallimu: ___ ad-darsa sahlun).

grammarPairs.rule: أَنَّ (anna) introduces an embedded reported clause and makes its noun accusative.
grammarPairs.example: Complete: أَخْبَرَنَا أَنَّ اللِّقَاء___ غَدًا (akhbaranā anna al-liqāʾ___ ghadan).

grammarPairs.rule: قَالَ لِـ (qāla li-) marks the person addressed.
grammarPairs.example: Complete: my father said to me — قَالَ ___ أَبِي (qāla ___ abī).

grammarPairs.rule: كَـ (ka-) — like is a preposition and makes the following noun genitive.
grammarPairs.example: Complete: knowledge is like light — اَلْعِلْمُ كَالنُّور___ (al-ʿilmu ka-n-nūr___).

grammarPairs.rule: كَأَنَّ (ka-anna) makes its noun accusative.
grammarPairs.example: Complete: كَأَنَّ الْقَمَر___ مِصْبَاحٌ (ka-anna al-qamar___ miṣbāḥun).

grammarPairs.rule: مِثْلُ (mithlu) behaves like a noun and its complement is genitive.
grammarPairs.example: Complete: this pen is like that pen — هٰذَا الْقَلَمُ مِثْلُ ذٰلِكَ الْقَلَم___ (hādhā al-qalamu mithlu dhālika al-qalam___).

grammarPairs.rule: In verb-first order, a verb before an explicit subject is usually singular.
grammarPairs.example: Complete: the students read the book — قَرَأَ الطُّلَّاب___ الْكِتَابَ (qaraʾa aṭ-ṭullāb___ al-kitāba).

grammarPairs.rule: In subject-first order, the verb normally shows full agreement with the subject.
grammarPairs.example: Complete: اَلطُّلَّابُ ___ الْكِتَابَ (aṭ-ṭullābu ___ al-kitāba) — the students read the book.

grammarPairs.rule: The explicit subject of a verb is nominative, even when it follows the verb.
grammarPairs.example: Complete: سَافَرَ الرِّجَال___ (sāfara ar-rijāl___) — the men traveled.

grammarPairs.rule: Many dialects use بِـ (bi-) before imperfect verbs for present or habitual meaning.
grammarPairs.example: Complete: he writes — هُوَّ ___ يَكْتُبْ in a dialect-style form.

grammarPairs.rule: عَمْ (ʿam) commonly marks progressive action in Levantine-style dialect phrases.
grammarPairs.example: Complete: I am studying — أَنَا عَمْ ___ (ana ʿam ___).

grammarPairs.rule: Dialect examples are useful for recognition, but formal writing should keep MSA endings and structures.
grammarPairs.example: Choose the formal MSA form for I write: أَكْتُب___ (aktub___).

grammarPairs.rule: The object of accompaniment follows وَ with the sense of with or alongside and is usually accusative.
grammarPairs.example: Complete with the correct case: جِئْتُ وَغُرُوبَ الشَّمْسِ

grammarPairs.rule: Ordinary وَ coordinates two equal roles; وَ of accompaniment introduces an accusative companion to the event.
grammarPairs.example: Choose the accompaniment reading: رَجَعَ الْأَبُ وَطُلُوعَ الْقَمَرِ

grammarPairs.rule: Purpose لِـ usually makes the following imperfect verb subjunctive.
grammarPairs.example: جِئْتُ لِأَتَعَلَّمَ (jiʾtu li-atʿallama)

grammarPairs.rule: Command لِـ takes a jussive imperfect and often means let someone do something.
grammarPairs.example: لِيَقْرَأْ أَخُوكَ (li-yaqraʾ akhūka)

grammarPairs.rule: مَا can be interrogative, negative, relative, or clause-forming; context determines the meaning.
grammarPairs.example: أَحْفَظُ مَا تَقُولُ (aḥfaẓu mā taqūlu)

grammarPairs.rule: After بَعْدَ, مَا can introduce a time clause meaning after something happens.
grammarPairs.example: سَأَزُورُكَ بَعْدَمَا يَنْتَهِي الدَّرْسُ

grammarPairs.rule: قَدْ plus a past verb often means already, have, or indeed.
grammarPairs.example: قَدْ فَهِمْتُ الدَّرْسَ (qad fahimtu ad-darsa)

grammarPairs.rule: قَدْ plus an imperfect verb often means may, might, or sometimes.
grammarPairs.example: قَدْ يَنْفَعُ الدَّوَاءُ (qad yanfaʿu ad-dawāʾu)

grammarPairs.rule: أَمَّا introduces a topic, and the following comment normally begins with فَـ.
grammarPairs.example: أَمَّا الْقِرَاءَةُ فَهِيَ مُفِيدَةٌ

grammarPairs.rule: أَمَّا ... فَـ is useful for contrast between two topics.
grammarPairs.example: أَمَّا الطَّالِبُ فَنَجَحَ، وَأَمَّا أَخُوهُ فَرَسَبَ

grammarPairs.rule: The basic quadriliteral verb pattern is فَعْلَلَ, with an imperfect like يُفَعْلِلُ.
grammarPairs.example: دَحْرَجَ يُدَحْرِجُ دَحْرَجَةً

grammarPairs.rule: Many تَفَعْلَلَ quadriliteral verbs describe the subject undergoing or doing the action by itself.
grammarPairs.example: تَدَحْرَجَتِ الْكُرَةُ (tadaḥrajati al-kuratu)

grammarPairs.rule: Form IX اِفْعَلَّ usually means to become a color or visible quality and is normally intransitive.
grammarPairs.example: اِحْمَرَّ وَجْهُهُ (iḥmarra wajhuhu)

grammarPairs.rule: The Form IX verbal noun often follows اِفْعِلَالٌ, such as اِحْمِرَارٌ.
grammarPairs.example: اِحْمِرَارُ الْوَجْهِ وَاضِحٌ

grammarPairs.rule: اِسْمُ الْآلَةِ names the tool used to perform an action, often on patterns like مِفْعَالٌ and مِفْعَلَةٌ.
grammarPairs.example: فَتَحَ becomes مِفْتَاحٌ

grammarPairs.rule: The preposition بِـ often marks the instrument used for an action.
grammarPairs.example: ضَرَبَ النَّجَّارُ الْمِسْمَارَ بِالْمِطْرَقَةِ

grammarPairs.rule: صِيَغُ الْمُبَالَغَةِ intensify active meanings and often show repeated or strong action.
grammarPairs.example: الْمُعَلِّمُ صَبُورٌ (al-muʿallimu ṣabūrun)

grammarPairs.rule: Intensive adjectives still agree for gender and number like other adjectives.
grammarPairs.example: امْرَأَةٌ صَبُورَةٌ (imraʾatun ṣabūratun)

grammarPairs.rule: Maqṣūr nouns end in long ā, and their case endings are usually estimated rather than visible.
grammarPairs.example: جَاءَ الْفَتَى، رَأَيْتُ الْفَتَى، مَرَرْتُ بِالْفَتَى

grammarPairs.rule: Indefinite manqūṣ nouns drop the final yāʾ in nominative and genitive but keep it in accusative.
grammarPairs.example: هٰذَا قَاضٍ، رَأَيْتُ قَاضِيًا

grammarPairs.rule: A sentence ḥāl describes the state of a definite participant and must link back to it.
grammarPairs.example: رَأَيْتُ الْمُدَرِّسَ وَهُوَ يَكْتُبُ (raʾaytu al-mudarrisa wa-huwa yaktubu)

grammarPairs.rule: وَاوُ الْحَالِ often introduces a nominal clause used as ḥāl.
grammarPairs.example: خَرَجَ الْوَلَدُ وَالشَّمْسُ طَالِعَةٌ

grammarPairs.rule: Tanāzuʿ occurs when two verbs compete for one visible noun that completes both meanings.
grammarPairs.example: حَضَرَ وَتَكَلَّمَ الْمُدِيرُ

grammarPairs.rule: A clearer alternative to tanāzuʿ repeats the noun once and then uses an attached pronoun.
grammarPairs.example: قَرَأْتُ الدَّرْسَ وَفَهِمْتُهُ

grammarPairs.rule: In ishtighāl, a fronted noun is resumed by a pronoun attached to the later verb.
grammarPairs.example: زَيْدًا رَأَيْتُهُ

grammarPairs.rule: Accusative ishtighāl often gives strong focus to the fronted noun.
grammarPairs.example: الْكِتَابَ قَرَأْتُهُ

grammarPairs.rule: Naʿt sababī agrees with the first noun in case and definiteness but follows the related noun in gender.
grammarPairs.example: رَأَيْتُ الرَّجُلَ الْجَمِيلَةَ بِنْتُهُ

grammarPairs.rule: The noun after a naʿt sababī often carries a pronoun linking it to the first noun.
grammarPairs.example: مَرَرْتُ بِطَالِبٍ حَسَنٍ خُلُقُهُ

grammarPairs.rule: وَلَا سِيَّمَا highlights one especially important member of a larger set.
grammarPairs.example: أُحِبُّ اللُّغَاتِ، وَلَا سِيَّمَا الْعَرَبِيَّةُ

grammarPairs.rule: After لَا سِيَّمَا, an indefinite highlighted noun is often learned in the accusative.
grammarPairs.example: نُكْرِمُ الضُّيُوفَ، وَلَا سِيَّمَا ضَيْفًا بَعِيدًا

grammarPairs.rule: بَلَى answers a negative question by cancelling the negation.
grammarPairs.example: أَلَسْتَ طَالِبًا؟ بَلَى

grammarPairs.rule: نَعَمْ is the ordinary yes for positive questions.
grammarPairs.example: هَلْ حَضَرَ عَلِيٌّ؟ نَعَمْ، حَضَرَ

grammarPairs.rule: In pause, most final short vowels and nunation are not pronounced.
grammarPairs.example: هٰذَا كِتَابٌ جَدِيدٌ

grammarPairs.rule: Accusative tanwīn in ـًا is commonly paused as a long ā sound.
grammarPairs.example: قَرَأْتُ كِتَابًا

grammarPairs.rule: A hamzated verb has hamza as one of its root consonants.
grammarPairs.example: قَرَأَ الْوَلَدُ قِصَّةً

grammarPairs.rule: Some common initial-hamza verbs have shortened imperatives.
grammarPairs.example: خُذْ هٰذَا الْكِتَابَ

grammarPairs.rule: Form VIII is based on اِفْتَعَلَ, but the inserted ت may assimilate to nearby sounds.
grammarPairs.example: اِضْطَرَبَ الْبَحْرُ

grammarPairs.rule: The verb اِتَّصَلَ comes from a root with initial wāw and belongs to Form VIII.
grammarPairs.example: اِتَّصَلَ الطَّالِبُ بِالْمُعَلِّمِ

grammarPairs.rule: Arabic often inserts a helping vowel when two sukūns meet in connected speech.
grammarPairs.example: قُلِ الْحَقَّ

grammarPairs.rule: The helping vowel usually disappears when the word stands alone.
grammarPairs.example: خُذْ، ثُمَّ خُذِ الْقَلَمَ

grammarPairs.rule: غَيْرُ and سِوَى make the following excluded noun genitive because they form an iḍāfa.
grammarPairs.example: سَافَرَ الْفَرِيقُ غَيْرَ لَاعِبٍ (sāfara al-farīqu ghayra lāʿibin)

grammarPairs.rule: When a preposition comes before غَيْرُ, غَيْرُ becomes genitive, and the noun after it remains genitive as an iḍāfa complement.
grammarPairs.example: جَلَسْتُ مَعَ غَيْرِ صَدِيقٍ (jalastu maʿa ghayri ṣadīqin)

grammarPairs.rule: A core Arabic preposition always governs the genitive, but its meaning depends on context and verb pairing.
grammarPairs.example: بَحَثَ عَنِ الْمِفْتَاحِ (baḥatha ʿani al-miftāḥi)

grammarPairs.rule: لِـ can show possession, benefit, or purpose; the following noun is genitive.
grammarPairs.example: هَذِهِ الْحَقِيبَةُ لِلْمُسَافِرِ (hādhihi al-ḥaqībatu lil-musāfiri)

grammarPairs.rule: Interrogative كَمْ asks how many and usually takes a singular accusative specification.
grammarPairs.example: كَمْ سَاعَةً دَرَسْتَ؟ (kam sāʿatan darasta?)

grammarPairs.rule: Khabariyya كَمْ means many or how many in an exclamatory sense, and its specification is commonly genitive.
grammarPairs.example: كَمْ بَابٍ فَتَحْتُ! (kam bābin fataḥtu!)

grammarPairs.rule: أَنْ plus a subjunctive imperfect verb can function like a verbal noun phrase.
grammarPairs.example: أُفَضِّلُ أَنْ أَكْتُبَ (ufaḍḍilu an aktuba)

grammarPairs.rule: A masdar muʾawwal can often be paraphrased with a regular maṣdar, though the wording and emphasis may change.
grammarPairs.example: يُفْرِحُنِي أَنْ تَحْضُرَ (yufriḥunī an taḥḍura)

grammarPairs.rule: Relative pronouns agree with a definite antecedent in gender and number, and dual forms also reflect case.
grammarPairs.example: الْبِنْتَانِ اللَّتَانِ قَرَأَتَا (al-bintāni allatāni qaraʾatā)

grammarPairs.rule: مَنْ and مَا can introduce general relative meanings without matching a specific definite antecedent.
grammarPairs.example: أُصَدِّقُ مَا تَقُولُ (uṣaddiqu mā taqūlu)

grammarPairs.rule: A bare diptote proper name does not take tanwīn and shows fatḥa for the genitive.
grammarPairs.example: سَكَنْتُ فِي مِصْرَ (sakantu fī miṣra)

grammarPairs.rule: The same diptote ending -a can mark accusative or genitive, so identify the governor.
grammarPairs.example: رَأَيْتُ فَاطِمَةَ (raʾaytu fāṭimata)

grammarPairs.rule: In direct comparison, اِسْمُ التَّفْضِيلِ commonly governs a مِنْ phrase.
grammarPairs.example: الطَّرِيقُ أَقْصَرُ مِنَ الشَّارِعِ (aṭ-ṭarīqu aqṣaru mina ash-shāriʿi)

grammarPairs.rule: When اِسْمُ التَّفْضِيلِ is used as a superlative of a group, the group often appears as a genitive iḍāfa complement.
grammarPairs.example: هَذَا أَجْمَلُ الْبُيُوتِ (hādhā ajmalu al-buyūti)

grammarPairs.rule: A fronted direct object keeps accusative case because its grammatical role does not change.
grammarPairs.example: الطَّعَامَ أَكَلَ الْوَلَدُ (aṭ-ṭaʿāma akala al-waladu)

grammarPairs.rule: إِيَّا forms are used for independent object pronouns, especially when the object is fronted.
grammarPairs.example: إِيَّاهَا أَعْرِفُ (iyyāhā aʿrifu)

grammarPairs.rule: Tamyīz al-nisba clarifies an entire relationship or judgment and is commonly indefinite accusative.
grammarPairs.example: زَادَ الطَّالِبُ اجْتِهَادًا (zāda aṭ-ṭālibu ijtihādan)

grammarPairs.rule: After comparatives and verbs of increase or decrease, the clarifying accusative often functions as tamyīz al-nisba.
grammarPairs.example: نَقَصَ الْمَاءُ مِقْدَارًا (naqaṣa al-māʾu miqdāran)

grammarPairs.rule: Ism al-marra names one occurrence of an action, often on فَعْلَةٌ for triliteral verbs.
grammarPairs.example: نَظَرَ نَظْرَةً سَرِيعَةً (naẓara naẓratan sarīʿatan)

grammarPairs.rule: Ism al-hayʾa names the manner, posture, or shape of an action, often on فِعْلَةٌ.
grammarPairs.example: مِشْيَتُهُ بَطِيئَةٌ (mishyatuhu baṭīʾatun)

grammarPairs.rule: Laysa negates a nominal sentence and makes its predicate accusative unless the predicate takes extra بِـ.
grammarPairs.example: لَيْسَ الدَّرْسُ صَعْبًا (laysa ad-darsu ṣaʿban)

grammarPairs.rule: The form لَيْسَ is fixed for third masculine singular, but other persons use forms such as لَسْتُ, لَسْنَا, and لَيْسُوا.
grammarPairs.example: لَسْنَا غَافِلِينَ (lasnā ghāfilīna)

grammarPairs.rule: Istighātha uses a vocative-like pattern to call a helper, often يَا لَـ... لِـ....
grammarPairs.example: يَا لَلْأَطِبَّاءِ لِلْمَرْضَى (yā la-l-aṭibbāʾi li-l-marḍā)

grammarPairs.rule: Nudba is a lamenting vocative, often introduced by وَا and sometimes ending with a long āh sound.
grammarPairs.example: وَا أَبَتَاهُ (wā abatah)

grammarPairs.rule: خَلَا, عَدَا, and حَاشَا may introduce exceptions; the following noun can be accusative if they act as verbs or genitive if they act as prepositions.
grammarPairs.example: حَضَرَ الطُّلَّابُ خَلَا طَالِبًا (ḥaḍara aṭ-ṭullābu khalā ṭāliban)

grammarPairs.rule: When مَا comes before خَلَا or عَدَا in exception, the following noun is normally accusative.
grammarPairs.example: نَجَحُوا مَا عَدَا طَالِبًا (najaḥū mā ʿadā ṭāliban)

grammarPairs.rule: Ḍamīr ash-shaʾn is a dummy pronoun explained by a complete sentence that follows it.
grammarPairs.example: عَلِمْتُ أَنَّهُ قَدْ حَضَرَ الْمُعَلِّمُ (ʿalimtu annahu qad ḥaḍara al-muʿallimu)

grammarPairs.rule: After ḍamīr ash-shaʾn, the explanatory sentence keeps its own subject and predicate or verb and subject.
grammarPairs.example: إِنَّهُ الصِّدْقُ مُنْجٍ (innahu aṣ-ṣidqu munjin)

grammarPairs.rule: Ighrāʾ urges the listener toward something good, often using an accusative noun with an understood command.
grammarPairs.example: الصَّبْرَ الصَّبْرَ (aṣ-ṣabra aṣ-ṣabra)

grammarPairs.rule: Taḥdhīr warns the listener away from danger, often with إِيَّاكَ وَ followed by an accusative noun.
grammarPairs.example: إِيَّاكَ وَالظُّلْمَ (iyyāka wa-ẓ-ẓulma)

grammarPairs.rule: In ʿaṭf, the coordinated noun usually follows the case of the noun it is joined to.
grammarPairs.example: مَرَرْتُ بِالطَّالِبِ وَالْمُعَلِّمِ (marartu bi-ṭ-ṭālibi wa-l-muʿallimi)

grammarPairs.rule: The meaning of each coordinating particle can differ, but the coordinated element still normally shares the syntactic case of what precedes it.
grammarPairs.example: سَأَلْتُ الْمُدِيرَ ثُمَّ الْمُوَظَّفَ (saʾaltu al-mudīra thumma al-muwaẓẓafa)

grammarPairs.rule: Spoken Arabic dialects often use fixed existential particles instead of MSA هُنَاكَ or يُوجَدُ.
grammarPairs.example: أَكُو كِتَاب، مَاكُو قَلَم (aku kitāb, māku qalam)

grammarPairs.rule: Egyptian negates the existential فِيه as مَفِيش, a fused form meaning there is not.
grammarPairs.example: مَفِيش مَكَان (mafīsh makān)

grammarPairs.rule: Egyptian demonstratives commonly follow definite nouns, especially دَه for masculine and دِي for feminine.
grammarPairs.example: الْبَيْت دَه (il-bēt da)

grammarPairs.rule: Many dialects build this plus noun with a ha- element attached to or placed before the definite noun.
grammarPairs.example: هَالْكِتَاب جَدِيد (hal-kitāb jadīd)

grammarPairs.rule: Colloquial dialects often use regional genitive markers where MSA would use iḍāfa or a possessive suffix.
grammarPairs.example: الْكْتَاب دْيَالِي (l-ktāb dyālī)

grammarPairs.rule: The genitive marker usually follows the possessed item and comes before the owner or possessive suffix.
grammarPairs.example: السَّيَّارَة مَال الْمُعَلِّم (is-sayyāra māl il-muʿallim)

grammarPairs.rule: Levantine expresses wanting with بَدّ plus pronoun endings, not with an MSA-style present-tense verb.
grammarPairs.example: بَدِّي مَيّ (baddī mayy)

grammarPairs.rule: Egyptian عَايِز changes for the speaker's gender: masculine عَايِز and feminine عَايْزَة.
grammarPairs.example: أَنَا عَايْزَة شَاي (ana ʿāyza shāy)

grammarPairs.rule: Dialect ability expressions are usually followed directly by the main verb, without MSA أَنْ.
grammarPairs.example: أَقْدَر أَسَاعْدَك (aʾdar asāʿdak)

grammarPairs.rule: Egyptian commonly negates ability with مَا...ش around أَقْدَر, producing مَاقْدَرْش.
grammarPairs.example: مَاقْدَرْش أَسْتَنَّى (maʾdarsh astannā)

grammarPairs.rule: Many dialects use r-w-ḥ forms for ordinary going, while Maghrebi commonly uses m-sh-y forms.
grammarPairs.example: بَرُوح عَالسُّوق (barūḥ ʿas-sūʾ)

grammarPairs.rule: Dialect go verbs usually take the destination directly or with a dialect preposition such as عَـ or لِـ.
grammarPairs.example: أَرُوح السُّوق (arūḥ is-sūʾ)

grammarPairs.rule: Hamzat al-waṣl is pronounced only when speech starts with it; hamzat al-qaṭʿ is pronounced everywhere.
grammarPairs.example: وَٱكْتُبِ ٱلْجَوَابَ (wa-ktubi al-jawāba)

grammarPairs.rule: Many imperatives from Form I begin with hamzat al-waṣl, such as ٱكْتُبْ and ٱفْتَحْ.
grammarPairs.example: ثُمَّ ٱفْتَحِ النَّافِذَةَ (thumma-ftaḥi an-nāfidhata)

grammarPairs.rule: The sound masculine plural is ـُونَ in the nominative and ـِينَ in both accusative and genitive.
grammarPairs.example: سَلَّمْتُ عَلَى الْمُعَلِّمِينَ (sallamtu ʿalā al-muʿallimīna)

grammarPairs.rule: The sound feminine plural uses kasra, not fatḥa, for both accusative and genitive endings.
grammarPairs.example: زُرْتُ مَكْتَبَاتٍ كَثِيرَةً (zurtu maktabātin kathīratan)

grammarPairs.rule: The particles لَمْ, لَمَّا, لَا النَّاهِيَةُ, and لِـ make the following imperfect verb jussive.
grammarPairs.example: لَا تَتَأَخَّرْ عَنِ الدَّرْسِ (lā tataʾakhkhar ʿani ad-darsi)

grammarPairs.rule: In the five verbs, the jussive is marked by deleting the final nūn.
grammarPairs.example: لَا تُهْمِلُوا الْوَاجِبَ (lā tuhmilū al-wājiba)

grammarPairs.rule: أَنْ, لَنْ, كَيْ, إِذَنْ, and purpose حَتَّى make the following imperfect verb subjunctive.
grammarPairs.example: أُحِبُّ أَنْ أَقْرَأَ كُلَّ يَوْمٍ (uḥibbu an aqraʾa kulla yawmin)

grammarPairs.rule: In the five verbs, the subjunctive is marked by deleting the final nūn, just like the jussive.
grammarPairs.example: لَنْ تُسَافِرُوا غَدًا (lan tusāfirū ghadan)

grammarPairs.rule: مَنْ and مَا are invariable shared relative nouns: مَنْ usually points to people, and مَا usually points to things or ideas.
grammarPairs.example: أَكْرِمْ مَنْ يُعَلِّمُكَ (akrim man yuʿallimuka)

grammarPairs.rule: A relative clause after مَنْ or مَا may need a return pronoun when the relative noun is not the clause subject.
grammarPairs.example: حَفِظْتُ مَا سَمِعْتُهُ (ḥafiẓtu mā samiʿtuhu)

grammarPairs.rule: In all iḍāfa types, the muḍāf has no tanwīn and no definite article, and the muḍāf ilayh is genitive.
grammarPairs.example: مِفْتَاحُ الْغُرْفَةِ (miftāḥu al-ghurfati)

grammarPairs.rule: A verbal iḍāfa often uses an adjective or participle as the first word and means X with respect to Y.
grammarPairs.example: رَجُلٌ طَوِيلُ الْقَامَةِ (rajulun ṭawīlu al-qāmati)

grammarPairs.rule: A khabar may be a single word, a nominal sentence, a verbal sentence, or a semi-sentence such as a prepositional phrase.
grammarPairs.example: الْمِصْبَاحُ فِي الْغُرْفَةِ (al-miṣbāḥu fī al-ghurfati)

grammarPairs.rule: A sentence predicate often contains a pronoun or verb form that connects it back to the mubtadaʾ.
grammarPairs.example: الْبِنْتُ أُمُّهَا طَبِيبَةٌ (al-bintu ummuhā ṭabībatun)

grammarPairs.rule: Ḍamīr al-faṣl is an independent pronoun inserted between a definite subject and definite predicate for separation and emphasis.
grammarPairs.example: الْحَقُّ هُوَ الْوَاضِحُ (al-ḥaqqu huwa al-wāḍiḥu)

grammarPairs.rule: The separating pronoun should match the first definite element in gender and number.
grammarPairs.example: الْجَامِعَةُ هِيَ الْمَسْؤُولَةُ (al-jāmiʿatu hiya al-masʾūlatu)

grammarPairs.rule: Some verbs such as أَعْطَى, مَنَحَ, عَلَّمَ, and كَسَا can take two accusative objects.
grammarPairs.example: مَنَحَ الْمُدِيرُ الْمُوَظَّفَ جَائِزَةً (manaḥa al-mudīru al-muwaẓẓafa jāʾizatan)

grammarPairs.rule: The first object of a two-object verb may be an attached pronoun, while the second object remains a visible accusative noun.
grammarPairs.example: أَعْطَيْتُهُ نَصِيحَةً (aʿṭaytuhu naṣīḥatan)

grammarPairs.rule: Verbs of transformation work like kāna: their subject is nominative and their predicate is accusative.
grammarPairs.example: أَصْبَحَتِ الْمَدِينَةُ مُزْدَحِمَةً (aṣbaḥati al-madīnatu muzdāḥimatan)

grammarPairs.rule: The predicate after صَارَ, أَصْبَحَ, أَمْسَى, بَاتَ, or ظَلَّ often describes the resulting state.
grammarPairs.example: ظَلَّ الْقَمَرُ ظَاهِرًا (ẓalla al-qamaru ẓāhiran)

grammarPairs.rule: After إِلَّا in an incomplete negative sentence, the following noun takes the case required by its role, not automatic accusative.
grammarPairs.example: مَا نَجَحَ إِلَّا الْمُجْتَهِدُ (mā najaḥa illā al-mujtahidu)

grammarPairs.rule: A complete affirmative exception with إِلَّا normally puts the excluded noun in the accusative.
grammarPairs.example: سَافَرَ الْمُوَظَّفُونَ إِلَّا مُوَظَّفًا (sāfara al-muwaẓẓafūna illā muwaẓẓafan)

grammarPairs.rule: Temporal لَمَّا and كُلَّمَا do not themselves make the following past verbs jussive.
grammarPairs.example: كُلَّمَا سَافَرْتُ تَعَلَّمْتُ شَيْئًا (kullamā sāfartu taʿallamtu shayʾan)

grammarPairs.rule: لَوْلَا is commonly followed by a noun and then an answer with لَـ showing what would have happened.
grammarPairs.example: لَوْلَا الْمُسَاعَدَةُ لَفَشِلْنَا (lawlā al-musāʿadatu lafashilnā)

grammarPairs.rule: Form I maṣdars have several patterns, so memorize common pairings such as كَتَبَ كِتَابَةً and دَخَلَ دُخُولًا.
grammarPairs.example: بَدَأَ دُخُولُ الطُّلَّابِ (badaʾa dukhūlu aṭ-ṭullābi)

grammarPairs.rule: A maṣdar can enter an iḍāfa and govern a following genitive noun.
grammarPairs.example: حِفْظُ الْكَلِمَاتِ نَافِعٌ (ḥifẓu al-kalimāti nāfiʿun)

grammarPairs.rule: A working active participle can take an accusative object, much like its verb.
grammarPairs.example: أَنَا حَافِظٌ قَصِيدَةً (anā ḥāfiẓun qaṣīdatan)

grammarPairs.rule: A passive participle can act like a passive verb and have a nominative deputy subject.
grammarPairs.example: أَمَقْرُوءٌ النَّصُّ؟ (a-maqrūʾun an-naṣṣu)

grammarPairs.rule: The jussive of a defective singular verb is formed by deleting the final weak letter.
grammarPairs.example: لَا تَنْسَ الْوَاجِبَ (lā tansa al-wājiba)

grammarPairs.rule: A fatḥa before the end often signals a deleted final alif in the jussive of verbs like يَخْشَى and يَنْسَى.
grammarPairs.example: لَمْ يَخْشَ الْمُسَافِرُ الطَّرِيقَ (lam yakhsha al-musāfiru aṭ-ṭarīqa)

grammarPairs.rule: Most regular nouns add an alif when they take accusative tanwīn, producing the spelling ـًا.
grammarPairs.example: شَرِبْتُ مَاءً وَأَكَلْتُ خُبْزًا (sharibtu māʾan wa-akaltu khubzan)

grammarPairs.rule: Words ending in tāʾ marbūṭa take fatḥatān directly on the tāʾ marbūṭa, without an added alif.
grammarPairs.example: قَرَأْتُ قِصَّةً جَمِيلَةً (qaraʾtu qiṣṣatan jamīlatan)

grammarPairs.rule: إِنَّ opens or emphasizes an independent statement; أَنَّ turns its clause into a noun-like complement meaning that.
grammarPairs.example: أَعْرِفُ أَنَّ الدَّرْسَ سَهْلٌ (aʿrifu anna ad-darsa sahlun)

grammarPairs.rule: After prepositions such as بِـ or لِـ, use أَنَّ, as in بِأَنَّ and لِأَنَّ.
grammarPairs.example: بَقِيتُ لِأَنَّ الْبَابَ مُغْلَقٌ

grammarPairs.rule: A mubtadaʾ or khabar may be omitted when context makes it obvious.
grammarPairs.example: أَيْنَ الْمُدِيرُ؟ فِي الْمَكْتَبِ

grammarPairs.rule: Short answers often keep only the new information and omit the repeated topic or predicate.
grammarPairs.example: أَيْنَ الْكِتَابُ؟ عَلَى الطَّاوِلَةِ

grammarPairs.rule: A prepositional phrase can function as ḥāl when it describes the state or manner of a definite owner.
grammarPairs.example: رَجَعَ الْمُسَافِرُ عَلَى تَعَبٍ

grammarPairs.rule: The prepositional phrase used as ḥāl is analyzed as being in the place of accusative, even though its noun is genitive after the preposition.
grammarPairs.example: دَخَلَتِ الْمُعَلِّمَةُ بِهُدُوءٍ

grammarPairs.rule: A plural of paucity can suggest a smaller set, while a plural of abundance can suggest a larger or more general set.
grammarPairs.example: عِنْدِي أَشْهُرٌ قَلِيلَةٌ

grammarPairs.rule: The paucity and abundance labels are traditional guides, but context controls the actual quantity in modern reading.
grammarPairs.example: مَرَّتْ شُهُورٌ كَثِيرَةٌ

grammarPairs.rule: When يَا is omitted, the noun remains vocative and keeps the same vocative case behavior.
grammarPairs.example: رَبِّ، ارْحَمْنِي

grammarPairs.rule: Omitted يَا is mostly a style choice; use explicit يَا when clarity matters.
grammarPairs.example: زَيْدُ، أَقْبِلْ

grammarPairs.rule: A relative clause needs a link back to its head noun; when the head is not the subject, that link is often an attached return pronoun.
grammarPairs.example: قَرَأْتُ الْكِتَابَ الَّذِي اشْتَرَيْتُهُ

grammarPairs.rule: After a preposition inside a relative clause, attach a pronoun that matches the head noun.
grammarPairs.example: زُرْتُ الْمَدِينَةَ الَّتِي وُلِدْتُ فِيهَا

grammarPairs.rule: إِذَا الْفُجَائِيَّةُ introduces a sudden scene, often after فَـ and before a nominal sentence.
grammarPairs.example: فَتَحْتُ الْبَابَ فَإِذَا صَدِيقِي وَاقِفٌ

grammarPairs.rule: Sudden إِذَا is normally followed by a nominal sentence that states the unexpected scene.
grammarPairs.example: بَحَثْتُ عَنِ الْمِفْتَاحِ فَإِذَا هُوَ فِي جَيْبِي

grammarPairs.rule: رُبَّ introduces an indefinite genitive noun and often gives the sense many a or sometimes.
grammarPairs.example: رُبَّ طَالِبٍ صَارَ عَالِمًا

grammarPairs.rule: رُبَّمَا is related to رُبَّ but usually introduces a verb clause with the meaning perhaps, sometimes, or often.
grammarPairs.example: رُبَّمَا يَتَغَيَّرُ الرَّأْيُ

grammarPairs.rule: Words ending in a vowel, N, or S stress the second-to-last syllable by default
grammarPairs.example: La palabra 'hablan' termina en N, entonces la sílaba acentuada es: ___

grammarPairs.rule: G before E/I = soft 'H' sound; J is always 'H'-like; H is always silent
grammarPairs.example: La palabra 'gente' (people) se pronuncia: ___

grammarPairs.rule: a + el = al, de + el = del (mandatory contractions)
grammarPairs.example: Voy ___ mercado. (a + el mercado)

grammarPairs.rule: No indefinite article with professions after ser — unless the profession is modified by an adjective
grammarPairs.example: Ella ___ enfermera. (She is a nurse — use the correct form of ser, no article)

grammarPairs.rule: Adjectives agree in gender and number with their noun; adjectives not ending in -o are invariable for gender
grammarPairs.example: La casa es ___ (big) y los jardines son ___ (beautiful, masc. pl.).

grammarPairs.rule: Nouns ending in -z change to -ces in the plural
grammarPairs.example: Tengo dos ___ en mi mochila. (lápiz, plural)

grammarPairs.rule: -ar verbs in present tense: stem + -o, -as, -a, -amos, -an
grammarPairs.example: Nosotros ___ (estudiar) español cada día.

grammarPairs.rule: Spanish present tense covers 'I speak', 'I am speaking', and 'I do speak'
grammarPairs.example: Ahora ___ (hablar, yo) con mi profesora.

grammarPairs.rule: -er and -ir verbs share most endings; nosotros differs: -emos (-er) vs -imos (-ir)
grammarPairs.example: Nosotros ___ (beber) agua y ___ (vivir) en la ciudad.

grammarPairs.rule: Negative sentences: place 'no' directly before the conjugated verb
grammarPairs.example: Ella ___ (not write) en su diario. (escribir)

grammarPairs.rule: Ser = identity/origin/profession/time/permanent traits; Estar = location/condition/ongoing action
grammarPairs.example: La fiesta ___ en mi casa. Yo ___ cansado.

grammarPairs.rule: 'Estar aburrido' = bored (state); 'Ser aburrido' = boring (personality)
grammarPairs.example: Esa película ___ muy aburrida. (The movie itself is boring as a trait)

grammarPairs.rule: Many verbs are irregular ONLY in yo: salgo, pongo, traigo, hago, conozco, doy, sé
grammarPairs.example: Yo ___ (salir) a las ocho y ___ (poner) la música.

grammarPairs.rule: Ir + a + infinitive = future plans ('going to'); Tener + que + infinitive = obligation ('have to')
grammarPairs.example: Mañana ___ (ir) a visitar a mi abuela y ___ (tener) que comprar flores.

grammarPairs.rule: Personal 'a' is required before specific people (and pets) as direct objects
grammarPairs.example: Llamo ___ mi hermana todos los días.

grammarPairs.rule: a + el = al (mandatory contraction); a + la stays separate — never contracts
grammarPairs.example: Voy ___ supermercado. (a + el)

grammarPairs.rule: In Latin America, 'ustedes' covers ALL plural 'you' — formal and informal
grammarPairs.example: ¿Cómo están ___? (asking a group of friends in Mexico City)

grammarPairs.rule: 'Qué' asks for definitions; 'cuál/cuáles' asks to choose from options
grammarPairs.example: ¿___ es tu número de teléfono? (asking someone to report their specific number)

grammarPairs.rule: All Spanish question words carry a written accent mark (tilde)
grammarPairs.example: ¿___ vives? (Where do you live?)

grammarPairs.rule: Object pronouns attach to infinitives, gerunds, and affirmative imperatives — or go before the conjugated verb
grammarPairs.example: ¿Puedes ___ el libro? (give it to me — IO me + DO lo, attached to the infinitive dar)

grammarPairs.rule: le/les become 'se' before lo/la/los/las — the sequence le+lo is forbidden
grammarPairs.example: ¿Le diste las llaves a Juan? Sí, ___ ___ di. (IO + DO)

grammarPairs.rule: Possessives agree with the THING owned in gender and number — not with the owner
grammarPairs.example: Tenemos ___ maletas listas para el viaje. (our — fem. pl.)

grammarPairs.rule: Short possessives mi/tu/su never change for gender — only for number (mi/mis, tu/tus, su/sus)
grammarPairs.example: Perdí ___ llaves y ___ cartera. (my keys, my wallet — both belong to me)

grammarPairs.rule: Neuter forms (esto/eso/aquello) refer to unidentified things or whole situations — they never modify a specific noun
grammarPairs.example: No entiendo ___. (referring to the whole situation — near-neutral distance)

grammarPairs.rule: Demonstratives agree in gender and number with the noun; use neuter forms (esto/eso/aquello) for vague references
grammarPairs.example: ___ estudiantes son de México. (these students — mixed group, plural)

grammarPairs.rule: The preterite of 'ser' and 'ir' are identical: fui, fuiste, fue, fuimos, fuisteis, fueron
grammarPairs.example: Ayer ___ al mercado con mi mamá. (went — ir)
